newsitem.title: ERITREA: Eritrea rules out joining Canadian-led force.
newsitem.headline: Eritrea rules out joining Canadian-led force.

text.p: Eritrea backed out of joining a planned multinational force for Zaire on Thursday because it will be led by Canada and Africa was not properly consulted.

"The U.N. Security Council said Canada will take command. It seems the secretary-general of the U.N. is passing by Africa, belittling and dismissing it," Eritrean Foreign Minister Petros Soloman told Reuters.
"The Canadians have a sad history in Somalia," he added.
Canada's peacekeeping record in Africa was sullied by the torturing and possible killing of Somalis in 1993 and a subsequent cover-up that is still being investigated in Canada.
Canadian command of the U.N. mission in Rwanda -- dealing with the same ethnic mix of Tutsis and Hutus -- failed to prevent the slaughter of a million people there in 1994.

"Eritrea's view is it is not willing to send a force to be commanded by the Canadians," said Petros, adding the U.N. Security Council should have cooperated with the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) rather than impose solutions on Africa.
Previously Eritrea was one of only seven African nations which agreed in principle to send troops to the force.
Petros said Eritrea was very critical of U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali's decision that Canada should lead the force because he had failed to consult Africans on the issue.
Eritrean President Isayas Afewerki told OAU Secretary-General Salim Ahmed Salim in a letter on Wednesday Eritrea was willing to send up to one brigade to Zaire.
Asked if he thought African nations could set up their own force, Petros said: "Our problem is not military capacity, we need the material support. A close coordination between forces is necessary".
African leaders have hit out at the U.N. for saying participating countries would bear the cost of the force.

"The whole point is African countries should be ready, and there should be a U.N. trust fund set up to fund the operation. I don't think there is a lack of countries willing to fund an operation like this," Petros said.

"Anyone can come but the Africans should be supported, first and foremost...It's becoming a private affair. Conflict solution is becoming something only the rich can afford. It is totally unacceptable," he said.
Eritrea, Africa's youngest nation, fought a 30-year guerrilla war against Ethiopia and became independent in 1993.
